questions.prompt: OpenAI's orchestration guide gives a starting rule for multi-agent design. What is it?

options.text: Give every department its own agent from the first day.
options.explanation: The guide warns that splitting too early creates more prompts, traces and approval points.

options.text: Start with one agent, and add specialists only when they clearly help.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's Building effective agents post gives the same advice: the simplest solution first.

options.text: Start with as many agents as the budget allows, then remove the slow ones.
options.explanation: Neither vendor recommends this. Both say add complexity only when it is needed.

questions.prompt: In which pattern does the main agent keep ownership of the final answer?

options.text: A handoff, where a specialist takes over the conversation.
options.explanation: In a handoff, control moves to the specialist agent.

options.text: Any pattern, because the first agent always writes the final answer.
options.explanation: Not true. In a handoff the specialist owns the next reply.

options.text: Agents as tools, where a manager calls specialists as helpers.
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's guide says the manager keeps ownership of the reply. Anthropic's orchestrator-workers pattern is similar.

questions.prompt: Anthropic's research post compares token use. What did it report?

options.text: Multi-agent systems used about 15 times more tokens than chat, so the task must pay.
options.explanation: Right. The post says agents used about 4 times more tokens than chat, and multi-agent systems about 15 times more.

options.text: Multi-agent systems used fewer tokens than chat because each agent has a smaller job.
options.explanation: The post reports the opposite: they burn through tokens fast.

options.text: Token use stayed about the same as in chat, but each run took more time to finish.
options.explanation: The post reports much higher token use, not the same.
